cities.d: in the east, the capital and largest city

x.around: In 2023, the Taliban-run traffic authority re-registered all taxi drivers in Afghanistan to reduce kidnappings and crimes involving unlicensed taxis. (As part of this change, all licensed taxis in the country were repainted from yellow to turquoise.) The initiative was deemed a success: Kabul police claimed that kidnappings had fallen "nearly to zero". Nowadays, being overcharged is your biggest threat.

hidden.d: A beautiful gallery in a charming old-Kabul house that has been carefully restored. The collection used to have 820 paintings and portraits but 50% have been looted or destroyed; the director said the Taliban destroyed 210…
This is the site where King Nadir Shah and his son, Zahir Shah, are buried. Restored in 2012 after being damaged during the wars.

n.en: Mausoleum of Nadir Shah and Zahir Shah

hidden.d: A centuries-old alleyway lined with cages filled with songbirds, fighting birds, and the occasional sickly bunny. Branching corridors leading to dilapidated courtyards where chickens are slaughtered by hand with a quick twist of…
A hill topped with television masts that offers great views of the city.

Open to the public on Tuesday afternoons and Fridays: football (soccer) with local Afghan guys, frisbee (with a collection of expats) and a 400 running track in comparatively green and pleasant surroundings.
Where foreigners are buried in Kabul. There are also memorial plaques commemorating those ISAF forces killed. Closed and padlocked as of 2026.
Guns, guns and more guns. Mostly rifles (and sewing machines, weirdly). Don't be shy – the dealers are happy to let you pose with the guns and take photos.
Walking along the city wall offers rewarding views over the city. The wall is still in pretty good condition, running west-east from Babur Gardens over to Bala Hissar (about 3 km in distance).

x.intro: Kabul is the capital and largest city of Afghanistan. A crowded metropolis pressed into a basin of the Hindu Kush mountains, its bazaars, battle-scarred buildings and traffic-choked streets bear the traces of an ancient trading city, rapid urban expansion, periods of cosmopolitan ambition, and nearly half a century of war.

must.d: The gardens surround the tomb of the first Mughal Emperor Babur. Though he had wished to be buried here, he was originally buried in Agra, and later moved to this spot.

Built as King Amanullah's Palace in the 1920s, it has been destroyed and rebuilt a few times over. By 2019, restoration works had been largely completed on the palace, which suffered massive damage during the 1990s civil war.
Not to be confused with Darul Aman, this palace was also built in the 1920 built to house the Royal family.

The zoo is very popular with Afghans, and houses over 100 animals, albeit in relatively poor condition. China was once one of the main donors of animals in the zoo, but after the death of a few animals to disease and…
Decorated with glazed tiles in a neo-Safavid Persian style, the building bears many inscriptions, including dedicatory texts, Qurʾanic excerpts, prayers, Hadith, and poetry.

Built in the late 19th century, it served as a summer palace for Amir Abdur Rahman. Today, much of the original interior has been preserved, and the area around the palace has become a large park. Under renovation as of 2026.
The National Archive contains numerous historic documents, with some on display in a small museum.

next.d: a village in a side valley of the Shamali Plain makes for an excellent overnight or day trip destination.
. This picturesque valley was one of many areas where the mujahideen resisted Soviet forces. Ruined tanks can be seen near the river and at the valley entrance.
and Band-e Amir National Park. One of the most beautiful regions of Afghanistan. Bamiyan is inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List and is particularly known for the two colossal Buddha statues…
. There are several daily and overnight buses. From Mazar-e Sharif you can visit nearby Balkh and go to Uzbekistan via Termez.
can be reached by taking a shared taxi (US$15, 2025) to the Torkham border crossing (traversing the famous Khyber Pass). From there take another shared taxi to Peshawar (Rs 2000, 2025).

x.safe: It’s common to encounter children begging for money, particularly in Shar-e Naw. While their requests may seem harmless, giving money can attract more children, quickly escalating into a crowd that’s difficult to manage. This can pose a safety risk, as it draws attention and may invite pickpocketing or other opportunistic crimes. To stay safe, politely decline and avoid engaging further.

cities.d: once one of the greatest cities in the region and capital of ancient Bactria. Although much of it lies in ruins, the remaining architectural and cultural elements are little changed since Alexander…

x.around: The town has a central park, where children play soccer or volleyball. At one end are the ruins of a tiled mosque; at the other, the gate of a madrassa. Again the construction technique of the madrassa can be seen. As the park is full of trees and small shops surround the park, it is difficult to take photos of the madrassa. Full shots of the mosque are easy. * * * * *

hidden.d: Also known as Bala Hasar, this shrine dominates the park in the centre of the town. It was built in the 15th century in the Timurid style.

n.en: Shrine of Khoja Abu Nasar Parsa

hidden.d: Well worth a visit. Its history is unclear but it is certainly one of Afghanistan's most important historical buildings.
A huge fortress built by the Timurid in the 15th century on the site of an Achaemenid fort where Alexander the Great married the beautiful Roxanne.
Remains of a Buddhist stupa. Accounts of Chinese Buddhist monk and traveler Xuanzang, who visited Balkh in 630 AD, indicate the existence of a significant number of Buddhist monasteries in the city.

cities.d: the remains of the Buddhas. Once considered one of the wonders of the world, these tall stone carvings were destroyed by the Taliban in a notorious act of cultural vandalism.

x.around: Bamiyan town is small and walking is the best option. Around the region you can hire Toyota minivans for day trips from the stand in front of Mama Najaf's Restaurant. Also, along the road in front of the large Buddha is the tourist office (in a pink building on the south side of the road) and you can hire a guide. The guide is well worth it for the money.

hidden.d: The ruined Buddhas are the main reason that most people visit Bamiyan. Although some feel that to visit at all is to reward cultural vandalism and desecration...
A ruined fortified citadel situated on a hill just east of Bamiyan, providing some of the best views of the entire valley.

x.intro: Bamiyan is the main town in Bamiyan Province. Bamiyan is one of the main tourist attractions in Afghanistan, largely due to the giant destroyed Buddha statues. It's also one of the most picturesque regions in the country. The "Cultural Landscape and Archaeological Remains of the Bamiyan Valley" is inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

next.d: one of the most stunningly beautiful natural sights in the whole country, these turquoise lakes are definitely worth the effort.

x.safe: Bamiyan is regarded as one of the safer destinations in Afghanistan. Its remoteness and the largely Hazara population have kept it distant from most of the fighting.

cities.d: in the south-east, between Kabul and Kandahar

must.d: Two elaborately decorated minaret towers, almost a thousand year old. The minarets are the remaining parts of a larger mosque.
Ruins of a former Buddhist monastery.

cities.d: in the west, gateway to Iran, has a strong Persian influence and several interesting historical sites

hidden.d: A very old and famous park near the mountain close to Gazar Gah.

The 4 minarets are all that remains of the medressa that he built. The new Iranian-built road cuts directly through them, two on each side. Most of the once beautiful blue tiling has vanished, though the floral outlines remain.
Jami was a very famous 15th-century Sufi poet. His tomb is highly revered, and popular with local women. To get here, walk roughly a kilometre north from the Baiqara minarets along the main road.
An overwhelming collection of weapons and military equipment left behind after Afghanistan's numerous invasions. Upstairs is a display in memory of the Soviet invasion.

x.intro: Herat (Dari: هرات) is a big, relatively wealthy city in western Afghanistan.

must.d: More than 800 years old, full of life and incredibly beautiful. Be sure and seek out the craftsmen's shop behind the main entrance, where you can watch them cut tiles and lay out new pieces for the building.

On a hill to the west of the old city, with great views overlooking the city. It has reopened to visitors after being used by the military to store ammunition for a few years, and is under restoration by the Aga Khan Trust for…

A large and famous Sufi shrine of Khoja Abdullah Ansari, tiled in blue with Kufic calligraphy. His tomb is the large blue structure at the back. There is no entrance fee, but donations are appreciated.
Once a mosque, a medressa, and a mausoleum, all that remains is a single, precariously tethered minaret and the large domed tomb of Gowhar Shad, who commissioned the original complex.
Housed in the Citadel the Herat National Museum, the collection is showcases the history of the region. However, many pieces have been either lost or looted.

x.safe: See the warning on the Afghanistan article for information on the security situation.

cities.d: in the east, between Kabul and the Khyber Pass

x.around: With plenty of greenery and water, Jalalabad is considered one of the most beautiful cities of Afghanistan. About 15 km from Jalalabad, a new city called Ghazi Amanullah Khan City is under development. Named after King Amanullah Khan, it is said to be the first, the biggest and the most modern city in the history of Afghanistan.

hidden.d: Tomb of Amānullāh Khān, who was the sovereign of the Kingdom of Afghanistan from 1919 to 1929, first as Emir and after 1926 as Malik (king).

x.intro: Jalalabad (Pashto: جلال آباد) is a city in eastern Afghanistan with a population of nearly 900,000 people.
x.safe: See the warning at the Afghanistan article for information on the security situation.

cities.d: a very conservative city in the south. Known as the home of the Taliban.

x.around: To get around the city visitors can use taxis or rent a vehicle, which usually comes with a reliable driver but special arrangements can be made to exclude the driver. The basic requirement for such special rental is insurance for the vehicle.
x.intro: Kandahar (Pashto: کندهار) is the capital of Kandahar province, and the largest city in Southern Afghanistan. Kandahar is also the second largest city in Afghanistan after the capital Kabul, and was the first capital of the modern state of Afghanistan in the 18th century.

must.d: One of the holiest sites in Afghanistan, contains what is said to be a cloak/robe worn by Prophet Mohammad during his famous night journey. The cloak is locked away inside and has not been taken out since 1996.

n.en: Mosque of the Cloak of the Prophet Mohammad

must.d: Resting place of Ahmad Shah Durrani, the founder of the state of Afghanistan.
Historical site located in the Sarpuza neighborhood. Climbing the 40 steps is dangerous. As such, children and elders should not climb them.
Contains the paintings of Ghiyassuddin, regarded as one of the most important Afghan painters of all time.

x.safe: See the warning on the Afghanistan article for information on the security situation.

intro: Although terrorist attacks have been declining, IS-KP attacks targeting foreigners still occur. Violence against women is widespread and in many cases legally sanctioned, and perpetrators are largely accorded impunity. Arbitrary arrest and detention, and widespread state violations of human rights, are among the worst in the world.

other.d: 5 stunningly turquoise lakes in a remote and beautiful setting not far from Bamiyan

x.around: Walking is pretty much the only way to get around the area once you arrive, unless you were to befriend the owner of a donkey or horse.
x.intro: Band-e Amir National Park (Persian: بند امیر) is the first national park of Afghanistan. It is a stunning group of turquoise lakes in the Eastern zone of the country, in Bamyan Province. It sits high in the Hindu Kush at an altitude of 2900m, and in 2013 about 6,000 local tourists visit the site each year. The area is protected by a small number of park rangers and most of the landmines are cleared.
x.safe: Land mines used to be prevalent around this area, especially along the road that leads in from Bamiyan. Most have been cleared, but to be safe anyway, stick to well-worn paths, and don't stray more than a couple of feet from the main access road.

other.d: the gateway to India and historic route of invasion and trade

x.around: Travelling by car or taxi is common. Traffic can be heavy and the roads are not in the best condition.

hidden.d: Located within the Landi Kotal Fort, this fascinating museum tells the story of the Khyber Rifles paramilitary force, with a treasure trove of artifacts and memorabilia.

x.intro: The Khyber Pass is the main route between Pakistan and Afghanistan. The pass is entirely within Pakistan. The nearest major cities on the route that goes over the pass are Jalalabad in Afghanistan and Peshawar in Pakistan, with Torkham as border crossing point.
x.safe: As of mid-2022, this area is considered extremely unsafe, as has been the case for well over a decade. See the warnings on the Pakistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa articles for more information. As of 2026, additionally, Pakistan is at war with Afghanistan.

other.d: well off the beaten path but some say worth the journey – possible as a roundtrip from Herat or when traversing the Central Route from Herat to Kabul

x.intro: Jam is a village in West Afghanistan, best known for the "Minaret of Jam".
